text: A quantum bit. A classical bit is either 0 or 1; a qubit can be in a blend of both at once, written α|0⟩ + β|1⟩. Every enemy in Bloch It! is a single qubit.
The angled bracket |…⟩ is called a 'ket'. It's how physicists write a quantum state: |0⟩ is 'the state zero', |ψ⟩ is 'some state ψ'. Part of Dirac's bra–ket notation.
The two states a qubit can be measured as. Any qubit state is a combination α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ of these two. In this game |0⟩ hurts you and |1⟩ is harmless.

A way to picture any single-qubit state as an arrow on a sphere. |0⟩ points to the north pole, |1⟩ to the south pole, and equal mixes like |+⟩ lie on the equator. Every single-qubit gate is a rotation of this sphere.
The quantum NOT. It swaps the two amplitudes: α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ → β|0⟩ + α|1⟩. On the Bloch sphere it is a half turn (180°) around the x-axis.
Looking at a qubit forces it to pick: it comes out as |0⟩ or |1⟩, at random, with probabilities set by its amplitudes. Your base measures each qubit that reaches it.
After a measurement the qubit is no longer in a blend. It has 'collapsed' into whichever result was seen, and its old amplitudes are gone.

The numbers α and β in α|0⟩ + β|1⟩. They can be negative or even complex, so they are not probabilities themselves; their squared sizes are. In the game, α is the top number on a qubit and β the bottom.
The chance of measuring |0⟩ is |α|² and of measuring |1⟩ is |β|². They always add up to 1. Your HP loss for each qubit is P(0) × 100 = |α|² × 100.
An operation that changes a qubit's state without measuring it. Gates are always reversible, and they never change the total probability. On the Bloch sphere, single-qubit gates are rotations.
Swaps the amplitudes like X, but also multiplies them by −i and i: α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ → −iβ|0⟩ + iα|1⟩. On the Bloch sphere it is a half turn around the y-axis.
The phase flip. It multiplies the |1⟩ amplitude by −1 and leaves |0⟩ alone, so the probabilities don't change. On the Bloch sphere it is a half turn around the vertical z-axis.
The number i with i² = −1. Amplitudes can be complex numbers like i/√2. Multiplying by i doesn't change a number's size, so it doesn't change any probability on its own.
A state with both α and β non-zero, such as 1/√2|0⟩ + 1/√2|1⟩. It isn't 'secretly 0 or 1': the two parts can interfere with each other until it's measured.

bloch.caption: From the pole |0⟩ to the equator: an equal superposition.

text: Mixes the two amplitudes: |0⟩ → |+⟩ and |1⟩ → |−⟩, and back again. On the Bloch sphere it is a half turn around the diagonal axis between x and z.
When a gate adds amplitudes together, equal signs reinforce and opposite signs cancel. This is how quantum algorithms make wrong answers vanish.
The sign (or complex angle) between α and β. |+⟩ and |−⟩ have identical probabilities but opposite phase. Measurement can't see it directly, but an H gate turns it into a real difference.

bloch.caption: Same probabilities, different phase: the arrow circles the equator.

text: |+⟩ = 1/√2|0⟩ + 1/√2|1⟩ and |−⟩ = 1/√2|0⟩ − 1/√2|1⟩. They sit on opposite sides of the Bloch sphere's equator, and H turns them into |0⟩ and |1⟩.
Mathematically, every quantum gate is a unitary matrix: it preserves the total probability |α|² + |β|² = 1, and it can always be undone.
Does nothing at all. The state passes through unchanged.
Multiplies the |1⟩ amplitude by i: a quarter turn around the z-axis. Two S gates make a Z.
Multiplies the |1⟩ amplitude by e^{iπ/4}: an eighth turn around the z-axis. Two T gates make an S.
Multiplies the |1⟩ amplitude by e^{iφ}: a turn of angle φ around the z-axis. Z, S and T are P(π), P(π/2) and P(π/4).
A two-qubit gate, also written CX. It flips the target (⊕) qubit only when the control (●) qubit is |1⟩. If the control is in a superposition, the two qubits become entangled.
A two-qubit gate. It multiplies the |11⟩ amplitude by −1. Which qubit is the control doesn't matter.
A two-qubit gate. It applies Y to the target qubit only when the control qubit is |1⟩. Because Y carries a factor of ±i, CY can untangle pairs whose shared state has an imaginary phase.
A two-qubit gate that trades the states of two neighbouring qubits, entanglement and all. It's built from three CNOTs, which is why it costs more than one.

bloch.caption: The two arrows trade places: SWAP moves each qubit's state into the other lane.

text: A state of three (or more) qubits that share one entangled state, such as 1/√2|000⟩ + 1/√2|111⟩. Measuring any one qubit fixes all the others. Oddly, any two of them on their own are only classically correlated: the entanglement belongs to the group as a whole. A CNOT can peel off one qubit at a time, leaving a smaller entangled state behind.

bloch.caption: Peeling a GHZ triad: the target goes free, and the other two stay as a Bell pair.

text: Two qubits are entangled when their joint state can't be split into one state for each. They no longer have amplitudes of their own, so the game colours them as a group and shows P(1) instead.
A maximally entangled pair, such as 1/√2|00⟩ + 1/√2|11⟩. Measuring one qubit instantly tells you what the other will be.

bloch.caption: |+⟩ and |0⟩ through a CNOT: out comes the Bell pair 1/√2|00⟩ + 1/√2|11⟩.
